newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Prices surge in balanced Budapest grains trade.
newsitem.headline: Prices surge in balanced Budapest grains trade.

text.p: The grains section of the Budapest Commodity Exchange saw an unusual pattern of balanced trade, high turnover and rising prices (BCE), dealers said.
"The buying and selling side was equally strong in a market that tends to be one-sided," said Ferenc Kiss of Agrokont.
He added that international trends and speculations were the main reasons for rising prices, but speculation could have played a more important role.
"Those players who have open selling positions try to keep prices high as the gains are cleared daily and the longer they can maintain the price the longer they can use those gains," Kiss said.
Most new (1997) crop milling wheat prices went limit-up to end between 23,350 forints per tonne for July and 26,600 forints for March.
Only May bucked the rising trend easing 20 forints to 26,380.
Milling wheat prices were freed up for October, December and January as they have had limit rises for five consecutive days, the BCE said.
Milling wheat accounted for 1,622 contracts out of a total grains turnover of 2,124 contracts or one billion forints, an the third highest daily turnover this year.
New crop feed wheat prices rose by the limit and September and October maturities were also freed up, as well as September barley.

Maize was the second most popular commodity with 305 contracts, and prices of all maturities went up mostly by the limit to end at 18,900 forints for May, 19,820 for December and 23,800 for July 1998.
However, Kiss said Thursday's price movements and high volumes were unlikely to be repeated on Friday.
"I think the market will calm down tomorrow," he said.
